question: Whether or not you loaded and secured the cargo yourself, which of the following is a stated driver responsibility?
choice_a: Determining the market value of the cargo
choice_b: Recognizing overloads and poorly balanced weight
explanation: The manual states that whether or not you load and secure the cargo yourself, you are responsible for inspecting your cargo, recognizing overloads and poorly balanced weight, knowing your cargo is properly secured and does not obscure your view, and knowing your cargo does not restrict access to emergency equipment.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: If you intend to carry hazardous material that requires placards on your vehicle, what do you also need?
explanation: The manual states that if you intend to carry hazardous material requiring placards, you will also need a Hazardous Materials endorsement, and that Section 9 of the manual covers the hazardous materials test.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: How soon after starting a trip should you inspect the cargo and its securing devices again?
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to inspect the cargo and its securing devices again within the first 50 miles after beginning a trip, and make any adjustments needed.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: Besides after every break you take, when else does the manual say you should re-check your cargo during a trip?
choice_a: After you have driven for 3 hours or 150 miles
choice_b: After you have driven for 1 hour or 50 miles
choice_c: Only at the end of the trip
choice_d: After you have driven for 6 hours or 300 miles
explanation: The manual lists re-checking cargo after you have driven for 3 hours or 150 miles, and after every break you take during driving, in addition to the initial 50-mile check.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: How does the manual define Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR)?
choice_a: The weight transmitted to the ground by one axle
choice_b: The maximum weight a tire can carry at a specified pressure
choice_c: The value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle
choice_d: The rated capacity of a suspension system
explanation: The manual defines Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR) as the value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: According to the manual, Gross Combination Weight Rating (GCWR) is generally:
choice_a: The weight of the cargo only, not including the vehicle
choice_b: The value specified by the manufacturer of the power unit, or the sum of the GVWRs or GVWs of the power unit and towed unit(s), whichever produces the highest value
choice_c: A fixed number set by federal law for all trucks
choice_d: The maximum weight a single tire can carry
explanation: The manual defines GCWR as the value specified by the manufacturer of the power unit if shown on the FMVSS certification label, or the sum of the GVWRs or GVWs of the power unit and towed unit(s), or any combination thereof, that produces the highest value.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: How does the manual define "axle weight"?
choice_a: The weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or one set of axles
choice_b: The manufacturer-rated capacity of the coupling device
choice_c: The loaded weight of a single vehicle
choice_d: The combined weight of the power unit and towed unit
explanation: The manual defines axle weight as the weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or one set of axles.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: What is the purpose of the bridge formula referenced in the manual's discussion of legal weight limits?
choice_a: To calculate fuel efficiency for combination vehicles
choice_b: To permit less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together, preventing overloading of bridges and roadways
choice_c: To determine the correct tire pressure for heavy loads
choice_d: To set the maximum speed limit for loaded trucks
explanation: The manual explains that maximum axle weights are often set by a bridge formula, which permits less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together, to prevent overloading bridges and roadways.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: According to the manual, what can overloading do to a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: It has no effect as long as tires are properly inflated
choice_c: It can hurt steering, braking, and speed control, and can cause brakes to fail from being forced to work too hard
choice_d: It only matters on flat, dry roads
explanation: The manual warns that overloading can have bad effects on steering, braking, and speed control; overloaded trucks must go slowly on upgrades, may gain too much speed on downgrades, have increased stopping distances, and brakes can fail when forced to work too hard.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

topic: Center of Gravity and Top-Heavy Loads
question: Why does the manual say it is important to distribute cargo as low as possible?
choice_a: A high center of gravity makes the vehicle more likely to tip over, especially in curves or when swerving
choice_b: It reduces wear on the tires only
choice_c: It makes the cargo easier to count
choice_d: It is required only for refrigerated cargo
explanation: The manual states that a high center of gravity (cargo piled up high or heavy cargo on top) means you are more likely to tip over, which is most dangerous in curves or if you have to swerve, so heaviest parts of cargo should be placed under the lightest parts.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: According to the manual, what is the minimum tie-down requirement for cargo on a flatbed trailer?
choice_a: One tie-down per twenty feet of cargo, with no minimum
choice_b: At least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, with a minimum of two tie-downs no matter how small the cargo
choice_c: Exactly four tie-downs regardless of cargo size
choice_d: One tie-down for the entire load, regardless of length
explanation: The manual states cargo should have at least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, and no matter how small the cargo, it should have at least two tie-downs.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Federal regulations require the aggregate working load limit of a cargo securement system to be at least:
choice_a: One-half times the weight of the article or group of articles being secured
choice_b: Equal to the weight of the article being secured
choice_c: Twice the weight of the article being secured
choice_d: One-quarter times the weight of the article being secured
explanation: The manual states that federal regulations require the aggregate working load limit of any securement system used to secure an article or group of articles against movement must be at least one-half times the weight of the article or group of articles.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What is the purpose of a front-end header board ("headache rack")?
choice_a: To improve the vehicle's fuel economy
choice_b: To protect the driver from cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop by blocking the forward movement of cargo
choice_c: To display the vehicle's weight rating
choice_d: To hold the tarp in place over the cargo
explanation: The manual states that front-end header boards protect the driver from cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop, and the front-end structure should block the forward movement of any cargo carried.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: What are the two basic reasons the manual gives for covering cargo?
choice_a: To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
choice_b: To hide the cargo from view and to reduce wind noise
choice_c: To keep the cargo warm and to reduce theft only
choice_d: To meet insurance requirements and to reduce vehicle weight
explanation: The manual gives two basic reasons for covering cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo, and to protect the cargo from weather.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: You cannot inspect the contents of a sealed load, but the manual says you should still check that:
choice_a: The seal number matches the bill of lading only
choice_b: You don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
choice_c: The container is painted the correct color
choice_d: The shipper has signed the manifest
explanation: The manual states that although you cannot inspect sealed loads, you should check that you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: According to the manual, why is livestock cargo dangerous even when it is bunched together with false bulkheads?
choice_a: Livestock can lean on curves, shifting the center of gravity and making rollover more likely
choice_b: Livestock always weighs more than the vehicle's rating
choice_c: Livestock cannot legally be transported by truck
choice_d: Livestock requires refrigeration equipment that adds excess weight
explanation: The manual explains that with less than a full load, false bulkheads should be used to keep livestock bunched together, but even when bunched, special care is necessary because livestock can lean on curves, shifting the center of gravity and making rollover more likely.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: What does the manual say may be required for over-length, over-width, and/or overweight loads?
choice_a: Nothing extra as long as the driver has a CDL
choice_b: Special transit permits, and possibly special equipment such as "wide load" signs, flashing lights, flags, or a police escort or pilot vehicles
choice_d: Only daytime driving is allowed, with no other restrictions
explanation: The manual states that over-length, over-width, and/or overweight loads require special transit permits, driving is usually limited to certain times, and special equipment may be necessary such as "wide load" signs, flashing lights, flags, and such loads may require a police escort or pilot vehicles.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3
